Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth two-dimensional Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary. For $x\in\partial M$, let $\nu_{\mathrm{out}}(x)$ be the outward unit normal. The boundary is **strictly convex** if
$$
g(\nabla_w\nu_{\mathrm{out}},w)>0
$$
for every $x\in\partial M$ and every nonzero $w\in T_x\partial M$. A **Jacobi field** along a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma$ is a smooth vector field $J$ along $\gamma$ satisfying
$$
D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0,
$$
where $R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$. The manifold has **no conjugate points** if, on every unit-speed geodesic segment $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$, a Jacobi field with $J(a)=J(b)=0$ must be identically zero. It is **nontrapping** if every maximal unit-speed geodesic starting in $M^\circ$ reaches $\partial M$ in finite forward and backward time. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **simple surface** if its boundary is strictly convex, it has no conjugate points, and it is nontrapping.

The unit tangent bundle is $SM=\{(x,v):x\in M,\ v\in T_xM,\ g_x(v,v)=1\}$. Write $\nu_{\mathrm{in}}=-\nu_{\mathrm{out}}$ and
$$
\partial_+SM=\{(x,v)\in SM:x\in\partial M,\ g_x(v,\nu_{\mathrm{in}})>0\}
$$
for inward-pointing unit boundary vectors. For $(x,v)\in\partial_+SM$, let $\gamma_{x,v}$ be the unit-speed geodesic with $\gamma_{x,v}(0)=x$ and $\dot\gamma_{x,v}(0)=v$, and let $\tau_+(x,v)$ be its first positive exit time from $M$. For $f\in C^\infty(M)$, its scalar **geodesic X-ray transform** is the function on $\partial_+SM$ defined by
$$
I_0f(x,v)=\int_0^{\tau_+(x,v)} f(\gamma_{x,v}(t))\,dt.
$$
The geodesic equation is interpreted up to first boundary exit; local smooth extensions of the metric are used only to solve the coordinate ODE at boundary initial data.

The **Riemannian volume density** is $\mu_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in coordinates.

The matrix is that of [[prop-coordinate-criterion-for-a-riemannian-metric]], so its determinant is positive and smooth. The density frames and their absolute-Jacobian law are [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]. In dimension zero take the empty determinant to be one, giving weight one at every point, independently of orientation. The compatibility of these local formulas is proved in [[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]].
Every supplied smooth Riemannian metric on a smooth manifold, including a manifold with boundary, has exactly one Levi–Civita connection. The construction adds no choice assumption.

For a supplied Riemannian metric $g$, a **Levi–Civita connection** is an affine connection on $TM$ that is both metric compatible and torsion free, in the senses of [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]], [[def-metric-compatible-connection-on-a-riemannian-vector-bundle]] and [[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]]. Thus for all local fields
$$Xg(Y,Z)=g(
abla_XY,Z)+g(Y,
abla_XZ),\qquad 
abla_XY-
abla_YX=[X,Y].$$
Existence and uniqueness are proved below from the supplied metric by the Koszul formula. This definition does not choose an arbitrary connection first and does not assume the general connection-existence theorem. In dimension zero the unique tangent-bundle connection satisfies both identities; in dimension one torsion freeness alone imposes no restriction, so metric compatibility remains essential.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$ and let $p\in M$. Then there exist
$h>0$, an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, and a smooth map

$$ \Phi:(-h,h)\times U\to M $$

such that for every $q\in U$, the curve $t\mapsto \Phi(t,q)$ is the unique
integral curve of $X$ on $(-h,h)$ with initial value $\Phi(0,q)=q$.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, let $I$ be a nondegenerate interval,
and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be an affinely parametrized geodesic. For a smooth
vector field $J$ along $\gamma$, write $D_tJ$ for its covariant derivative
along $\gamma$ and $D_t^2J=D_t(D_tJ)$, using
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]. The curvature operator $R$ has the
convention
$$R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z,$$
as fixed by [[lem-covariant-derivatives-commute-up-to-curvature-in-a-two-parameter-variation]]
and used in [[def-riemann-curvature-four-tensor]]. A smooth field $J$ is a
**Jacobi field** along $\gamma$ when it satisfies the Jacobi equation
$$D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0$$
throughout $I$. We write $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ for the set of these fields.

The interval is required to have nonempty interior so that the covariant
derivatives are defined; if an endpoint is included, the equation there uses
the one-sided derivatives of the smooth field. Constant geodesics are included:
when $\dot\gamma=0$, the curvature term vanishes and the equation is
$D_t^2J=0$. On a zero-dimensional manifold the only field is zero, so the
equation holds. In dimension one the same equation and curvature convention
apply without a separate restriction. The definition classifies a specified
field and geodesic and makes no existence choice.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $\nabla$ be an affine connection on $M$ in
the sense of [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]], and let $X,Y,Z$ be
smooth vector fields. With the sign convention used throughout this page, the
**curvature of $\nabla$** is

$$R^\nabla(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z,$$

where $[X,Y]$ is the bracket of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. We usually write $R$ when the
connection is understood. The connection is **flat** or **curvature-free** when
$R(X,Y)Z=0$ for every triple of smooth vector fields.

The bracket correction is part of the definition. The raw commutator of two
covariant derivatives is not function-linear in its differentiating fields.
No metric or torsion hypothesis is imposed here. On an empty or
zero-dimensional manifold the condition is vacuous; on manifolds with boundary
the same formula uses the ambient tangent bundle supplied by the definition of
an affine connection.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, let $\nabla$ be its unique
Levi–Civita connection, and let $R$ be the curvature tensor with the sign fixed
above. The **Riemann curvature four-tensor** is the covariant tensor

$$\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W):=g(R(X,Y)Z,W).$$

Thus the first two arguments are the two differentiating slots, the third is
the field acted on, and the fourth lowers the output index. In coordinates,
if $R(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_k=R^m{}_{kij}\partial_m$, then
$R_{ijkl}=g_{lm}R^m{}_{kij}$ under this argument order. This convention makes
$\operatorname{Rm}(u,v,v,u)$ positive on a positively curved round sphere.

The definition uses no chosen frame. On an empty or zero-dimensional manifold
it gives the unique zero four-tensor; in dimension one the same formula applies
and later symmetries force it to vanish. It is valid up to the boundary when a
Riemannian manifold with boundary is supplied.

A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that $g_p(v,v)>0$ for every point $p$ and every nonzero $v\in T_pM$. A **Riemannian manifold** is the pair $(M,g)$.

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The empty manifold has its unique empty metric. Boundaries are allowed where stated, with smoothness understood up to the boundary.

The **Riemannian speed** on a $C^1$ piece is $|\dot\gamma(t)|_g=\sqrt{g_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))}$. Its **length** is $L_g(\gamma)=\sum_j\int_{t_{j-1}}^{t_j}|\dot\gamma(t)|_g\,dt$.

The curve convention is [[def-piecewise-c-one-curve-on-a-manifold]] and the norm is [[def-pointwise-norm-and-angle-from-a-riemannian-metric]]. Each integrand is continuous on its closed piece with the one-sided endpoint derivative, hence Riemann integrable and nonnegative. Values chosen at the finitely many corners do not change its integral. For a singleton interval the empty sum is zero; a constant curve also has zero length. Partition independence is established by [[lem-riemannian-length-is-independent-of-piecewise-c-one-subdivision]].

On a connected Riemannian manifold define $d_g(p,q)=\inf\{L_g(\gamma):\gamma\text{ is piecewise }C^1\text{ from }p\text{ to }q\}$.

Lengths are those of [[def-riemannian-speed-and-length]]. For each pair $p,q$, [[lem-any-two-points-in-a-connected-smooth-manifold-can-be-joined-by-a-piecewise-c-one-curve]] supplies a curve, so the set of lengths is nonempty, contains a finite real number and is bounded below by zero. Applying the least-upper-bound property [[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]] to the negatives gives a finite nonnegative infimum. On the empty connected manifold this defines the empty distance function; there are no pairs to evaluate. No minimizing curve is part of this definition.
$d_g$ is a finite metric on a connected Riemannian manifold.
The topology of $d_g$ is the manifold topology on every connected Riemannian manifold.
For every piecewise $C^1$ curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$, $d_g(\gamma(a),\gamma(b))\le L_g(\gamma)$.

A change of positive orthonormal frame changes $\theta$ by a smooth rotation angle depending on $x$; its coordinate Jacobian is triangular with fibre derivative $1$, so this density is independent of the frame.

The local ODE result in [F4] gives unique geodesic arcs with smooth dependence on initial state. The coordinate equations agree on overlaps because they are the covariant equation $D_t\dot\gamma=0$; metric compatibility gives $\frac{d}{dt}g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=2g(D_t\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=0$. Thus the local arcs patch uniquely on their common intervals and unit-speed initial states remain in $SM$ until exit.

The horizontal lifts are $H_i=e_i-\omega(e_i)V$ and $X=\cos\theta\,H_1+\sin\theta\,H_2$. At fixed $\theta$, the base divergence of $v$ is $\operatorname{div}_g v=\omega(v^\perp)$, while the vertical coefficient of $X$ is $-\omega(v)$ and its $\theta$-derivative is $-\omega(v^\perp)$. Hence $\operatorname{div}_{d\Sigma}X=0$. Also $\operatorname{div}_{d\Sigma}V=0$ because $V=\partial_\theta$, and $\operatorname{div}_{d\Sigma}X^\perp=0$ because $X^\perp=[X,V]$ and $\operatorname{div}[X,V]=X(\operatorname{div}V)-V(\operatorname{div}X)$. The local flow equation for the density is $\frac{d}{dt}\varphi_t^*d\Sigma=\varphi_t^*(\operatorname{div}_{d\Sigma}X\,d\Sigma)=0$, so the geodesic flow preserves $d\Sigma$ until boundary exit.

Write $\omega_i=\omega(e_i)$. The curvature definition gives $R(e_1,e_2)e_1=d\omega(e_1,e_2)e_2$ and $R(e_1,e_2)e_2=-d\omega(e_1,e_2)e_1$, so $d\omega=-K\,dV_g$ for $K=g(R(e_1,e_2)e_2,e_1)$. First-slot skewness follows from [F6]; last-slot skewness follows by applying metric compatibility in [F3] to $g(R(A,B)C,D)+g(C,R(A,B)D)$. Under a positive rotation of $(e_1,e_2)$, each alternating pair in $g(R(e_1,e_2)e_2,e_1)$ is multiplied by the determinant $1$, so $K$ is frame-independent. Torsion-freeness gives $[e_1,e_2]=-\omega_1e_1-\omega_2e_2$ and direct expansion of $H_i=e_i-\omega_iV$ gives $[H_1,H_2]=-\omega_1H_1-\omega_2H_2+KV$. The unit circle bundle $SM$ is compact: cover compact $M$ by finitely many smaller coordinate neighborhoods with closures inside charts carrying smooth orthonormal frames; each part of $SM$ over such a closure is homeomorphic to the product of that compact closure with $S^1$, so finitely many compact sets cover $SM$. These disjoint sets are compact in the metric topology by [F7], so the minimum is attained and is positive because $d_g$ is a metric. For a subset $A$, write $d_g(x,A)=\inf_{a\in A}d_g(x,a)$.

Consequently $\mathcal I_\gamma(Y,Y)=\int_0^L j^2(q')^2dt\ge0$, with equality only if $q$ is constant and hence zero from $q(L)=0$. Thus the index form is positive definite.

If $d_g(x,\partial M)<D/4$, the triangle inequality gives $d_g(x,\operatorname{supp}f)>3D/4$; hence a unit-speed curve from $x$ cannot reach the support before time $D/2$, since its length equals elapsed time and endpoint distance is at most length. Fix any $z=(x,v)\in\partial SM$ and a boundary chart with defining coordinate $\rho$ positive inside. If $v$ is transverse, choose the one of $v,-v$ pointing outward; after shrinking a neighborhood, $\rho'(t)<-c<0$ up to some $t_0<D/2$, and nearby interior states have $\rho(0)<ct_0$, so this ray exits by $t_0$. If $v$ is tangent, step 3.1 gives $\rho''(0)<0$. Choose $t_0<D/2$ small enough to remain in the chart; after shrinking a neighborhood, $\rho''(t)<-c<0$ for $0\le t\le t_0$, while $\rho(0)<ct_0^2/8$ and $|\rho'(0)|<ct_0/4$. Taylor's formula yields $\rho(t_0)\le\rho(0)+t_0\rho'(0)-ct_0^2/2<0$, so the geodesic has exited by $t_0$. In either case there is a neighborhood of $z$ and one fixed orientation whose forward ray exits before reaching $\operatorname{supp}f$. Shrink each such neighborhood so every state in it also has base point at distance less than $D/4$ from $\partial M$. Compactness of $\partial SM$ from step 3.4 gives a finite subcover, whose union contains an open neighborhood of $\partial SM$ with the same property.

Away from tangent boundary states, step 3.1 gives transverse exit, so the implicit function theorem and smooth ODE dependence make $u_f$ smooth. In the neighborhood from step 4.3, one of $u_f(x,v)$ and $u_f(x,-v)$ is zero by the support separation. Their sum is the full boundary-to-boundary integral of $f$ along the same unoriented geodesic, which is $I_0f=0$ by [F1]; therefore both vanish throughout that neighborhood. Thus $u_f$ is zero near $\partial SM$, removing the glancing singularity and making it smooth with compact support in $SM^\circ$, since $SM$ is compact by step 3.4. Along the flow, $u_f(\varphi_s(x,v))=\int_s^{\tau_+(x,v)}f(\varphi_t(x,v))dt$, so differentiation gives $Xu_f=-f$. The incoming boundary value is $I_0f=0$ and the outgoing value is zero because its future exit time is zero.

Let $M$ be a smooth two-dimensional manifold with boundary and let $\det T_xM=\Lambda^2T_xM$ be the determinant line of its tangent space. An orientation of $T_xM$ is a positive ray $o_x$ in this line. The **tangent orientation double cover** is the set
$$
\widetilde M=\{(x,o_x):x\in M,\ o_x\text{ is an orientation of }T_xM\},\qquad \pi(x,o_x)=x.
$$
For a boundary chart $\phi:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb H^2$, let $o_\phi(x)$ be the ray obtained by applying $\det(d\phi_x^{-1})$ to the standard positive ray in $\det\mathbb R^2$. Give $\widetilde M$ the smooth boundary-chart structure whose two local sheets over $U$ are $\{(x,o_\phi(x)):x\in U\}$ and $\{(x,-o_\phi(x)):x\in U\}$, each with coordinate map $(x,\pm o_\phi(x))\mapsto\phi(x)$. On an overlap with a second chart $\psi$, the sheet sign changes by $\operatorname{sgn}\det D(\psi\circ\phi^{-1})$; this sign is locally constant, so the sheet transitions are smooth half-space transitions. Thus $\pi$ is the associated two-sheeted smooth covering map, including over the boundary. The involution $\tau(x,o_x)=(x,-o_x)$ exchanges the sheets. The canonical orientation of $\widetilde M$ at $(x,o_x)$ is the ray $(\det d\pi_{(x,o_x)})^{-1}(o_x)$ in $\det T_{(x,o_x)}\widetilde M$.
If $p:E\to B$ is a finite-sheeted covering, then $E$ is compact if and only if $B$ is compact.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $\pi$ is a two-sheeted covering; applying [F3] to compact $M$ shows that $\widetilde M$ is compact. In each boundary chart the two sheets are copies of the same half-space chart, so $\pi^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial\widetilde M$ and $\pi^{-1}(M^\circ)=\widetilde M^\circ$.

Every connected component $C$ of the smooth manifold $\widetilde M$ is open, since each point has a connected chart neighborhood contained in its component, and it is closed, since connected components are closed. Thus $C$ is compact. Smooth boundary charts have path-connected smaller half-ball neighborhoods, so $M$ is locally path-connected and [F8] makes connected $M$ path-connected. Fix $\widetilde x\in C$ and any $y\in M$; lift a path from $\pi(\widetilde x)$ to $y$ starting at $\widetilde x$ by [F6]. Its connected image stays in $C$, so its endpoint lies over $y$ and $\pi(C)=M$. The canonical orientation from [F2] restricts to $C$.

The pullback $\widetilde g=\pi^*g$ is smooth and positive definite because $d\pi$ is a smooth isomorphism on each sheet and $g$ is smooth positive definite by [F4]. In the sheet coordinates of [F2], $\pi$ is the identity and the metric coefficient matrices of $\widetilde g$ and $g$ coincide. The unique Levi-Civita connections therefore have identical coordinate coefficients; the geodesic equations and curvature coefficients also coincide by [F4, F5]. Boundary normals and their second fundamental forms correspond under $d\pi$, so strict convexity of $\partial M$ gives strict convexity of $\partial C$.

If $\widetilde J$ vanishes at both endpoints, its projection vanishes there; [F1] makes the projected field zero, and invertibility of $d\pi$ gives $\widetilde J=0$. A unit-speed geodesic in $C^\circ$ projects by step 2.1 to a unit-speed geodesic in $M^\circ$. By [F1] that projected geodesic reaches $\partial M$ in finite forward and backward time. Lift each finite projected segment from the specified initial point by [F6]. In every sheet the lift solves the same geodesic ODE as the original curve, so uniqueness from [F7] makes it an extension of that curve to the exit time; the endpoint lies in $\partial C$ by step 1.1. $$

It is **nontrapping** if every maximal unit-speed geodesic starting in $M^\circ$ reaches $\partial M$ in finite forward and backward time. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **simple surface** if its boundary is strictly convex, it has no conjugate points, and it is nontrapping.

The unit tangent bundle is $SM=\{(x,v):x\in M,\ v\in T_xM,\ g_x(v,v)=1\}$. Write $\nu_{\mathrm{in}}=-\nu_{\mathrm{out}}$ and
$$
\partial_+SM=\{(x,v)\in SM:x\in\partial M,\ g_x(v,\nu_{\mathrm{in}})>0\}
$$

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty, oriented smooth Riemannian surface with smooth strictly convex boundary, no conjugate points, and nontrapping geodesic flow. For $w\in C^\infty(SM)$ define the geodesic vector field by $Xw=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{0}w(\varphi_t(x,v))$. Define the vertical vector field by $Vw(x,v)=\left.\frac{d}{d\theta}\right|_{0}w(x,\cos\theta\,v+\sin\theta\,v^\perp)$, where $v^\perp$ is the positive $90$-degree rotation of $v$, and put $X^\perp=[X,V]$. derivations.claim: Since $V$ rotates the vector within its fixed fibre, it is tangent to $\partial SM$. The restriction of $u$ to $\partial SM$ is zero, so its derivative along every tangent vector there is zero; hence $Vu=0$ on $\partial SM$. In particular, the boundary products $(Vu)(X^\perp u)$ and $(Vu)(Xu)$ vanish, as needed for the $X$ and $X^\perp$ integration-by-parts formulas in [F3].
Put $P=XVu$ and $Q=X^\perp u$. From $[X,V]=XV-VX=X^\perp$ we have $VXu=P-Q$, and therefore $\|VXu\|^2=\|P\|^2-2(P,Q)+\|Q\|^2$.

Integrating $X$ by parts with boundary factor $(Vu)(X^\perp u)=0$, then using $XX^\perp=X^\perp X-KV$, gives $(P,Q)=-(Vu,XX^\perp u)=-(Vu,X^\perp Xu)+(KVu,Vu)$. Integrating $X^\perp$ by parts with boundary factor $(Vu)(Xu)=0$ turns the first term into $(X^\perp Vu,Xu)$.

The commutator $[V,X^\perp]=X$ implies $X^\perp Vu=VX^\perp u-Xu$. Thus $(X^\perp Vu,Xu)=(VX^\perp u,Xu)-\|Xu\|^2=-(X^\perp u,VXu)-\|Xu\|^2$, where the last equality is integration by parts for $V$, whose vector field is tangent to $\partial SM$. As $VXu=P-Q$, this gives $(P,Q)=-(Q,P-Q)-\|Xu\|^2+(KVu,Vu)=-(P,Q)+\|Q\|^2-\|Xu\|^2+(KVu,Vu)$. Solving gives $2(P,Q)=\|Q\|^2-\|Xu\|^2+(KVu,Vu)$.
Substitute this value in step 2.1 and cancel $\|Q\|^2$. The result is $\|VXu\|^2=\|P\|^2+\|Xu\|^2-(KVu,Vu)=\|XVu\|^2-(KVu,Vu)+\|Xu\|^2$, which is the asserted identity.
